rashi:a2.1: But this depends on that: it is a refutation that he raises.
rashi:a3.1: He stands in violation of a positive mitzva: with a sin offering and with a guilt offering alike he stands in violation of a positive mitzva, since “Only your holy things” implies: these are the substitutes of a burnt offering and a peace offering, and their offspring and their substitutes, as it is written after it, “And you shall offer your burnt offerings” etc., and not other sacrificial animals, such as a sin offering and a guilt offering. And a prohibition that comes by implication from a positive mitzva has the status of a positive mitzva.
rashi:a4.1: But this halakha was learned as a tradition: that in any case where a sin offering is left to die, with a guilt offering it grazes; the substitute of a sin offering dies, so that of a guilt offering grazes, and when it becomes blemished its money goes to communal gift offerings, that is, a burnt offering.
rashi:a5.1: A guilt offering that was consigned to grazing: if [the court] handed it over to the shepherd, and he went ahead and slaughtered it unspecified before it became blemished, it is valid as a burnt offering, since when unspecified it stands for the sake of a burnt offering with regard to its value.
rashi:a6.1: Not consigned, no: and even though its owner has achieved atonement [with another animal], since it has not yet been consigned by ruling to grazing, if he slaughtered it unspecified it is entirely disqualified.
rashi:a6.2: What is the reason? Because the verse states “It is”: it shall remain in its present state. It is still a guilt offering, and it is not fit to be sacrificed as a guilt offering; therefore it is disqualified.
rashi:a8.1: And let him derive all of them from it: since we expounded all of them from it above.
rashi:a9.1: “You shall take and go”: even from their grazing. This “you shall take and go” does not come for offspring and substitutes but for the sacrificial animals themselves, warning him to bring them even if they are at pasture in the meadow and the time of the Festival has come to go up. He should not say: I will not trouble myself to seek them in the marsh and bring them, but I will wait until another time.
rashi:a9.2: Another version: even from their threshing-boards [morigim]: even if they are threshing grain with threshing-boards, as we say in Menaḥot, in the chapter HaKometz Rabba (Menaḥot 22a): What are morigim? “Izei dekurkesa” with which they thresh. [That is,] a large perforated board with pegs set in it; they lay it on the grain and drive the animals over it. And the verse comes to say: if the animal you wish to consecrate is threshing, and you are about to go up for the Festival, do not say, since it is threshing I will wait until another time; rather, take it and go.
rashi:a10.1: MISHNA: It is not sacrificed as a peace offering: rather, it is placed in a vaulted chamber and dies. And this is by rabbinic law, because of the decree [explained] below, since certainly from Sinai only the five sin offerings that are left to die were learned.
rashi:a11.1: They do not disagree about the offspring of the offspring of a peace offering and about the offspring of the offspring of a substitute: the Gemara explains it.
rashi:a13.1: GEMARA: “And if [ve’im] a sacrifice of peace offerings”: he expounds this “im” as if it were “em” [mother], with a tzere.
rashi:a14.1: And its replacement: for example, it was lost, and he separated another in its place, and the first was found, and now both of them stand [before him].
rashi:a14.2: The verse states “If for a thanksgiving”: this “if” includes all of them, that they are sacrificed, and Rabbi Eliezer does not disagree.
rashi:a15.1: A decree: if you say that the offspring of a peace offering has a remedy, he will come to keep the mother back until it gives birth, and raise herds from the offspring, and come through them to shearing and labor [with consecrated animals]. And with a thanks offering, the reason he did not decree is that a thanks offering is not as common as a peace offering.
rashi:a17.1: How is it taught? Is this “that it is not sacrificed,” which Rabbi Shimon says, the beginning of his statement, so that he is saying: they do not disagree such that Rabbi Eliezer would say it is not sacrificed; rather, certainly it is sacrificed? Or is it the end of his statement, so that he is saying: they do not disagree, since certainly it is not sacrificed, even according to the Rabbis? [The question is:] does Rabbi Eliezer concede in this case, where they are found to have generations, or not? [With the offspring of the offspring,] they are found to have generations, so a person does not remember that they came from a peace offering, and there is no need to decree lest others see that this one sacrifices them and delay their own peace offerings for the sake of the offspring, to raise herds from them.
rashi:a18.1: It is merely a chance: it is not common to delay it so long.
tosafot:a4.1: Why do I need a verse; but this halakha was learned as a tradition: And if you will say: let him answer as above, that the verse is needed for where he transgressed and sacrificed, that he stands in violation of a positive mitzva. One can say: [“it is”] does not imply a positive mitzva as strongly as “only” does.
tosafot:a6.1: In brief: Rashi’s text reads: “Consigned, yes; not consigned, no. What is the reason? ‘It is’: it shall remain in its present state.” Tosafot finds this difficult on two counts. First, here consigning is required by a verse, while in Pesaḥim, in the chapter Elu Overin (73a), consigning is required only as a decree: Rav Huna said that Rav said, a guilt offering consigned to grazing and slaughtered unspecified is valid as a burnt offering, so no uprooting [of its name] is needed; then why specify consigned, when even not consigned it should be valid? And the answer there is: a decree [before atonement, on account of after atonement]. Second, here it says the animal is valid as a burnt offering, while throughout the Talmud the halakha to Moses from Sinai is that wherever a sin offering dies, a guilt offering grazes. Therefore Rabbeinu Tam holds that the halakha to Moses from Sinai concluded that with a guilt offering it is offered as a burnt offering, and here one does not read “consigned, yes; not consigned, no.” Rather the text reads: a guilt offering consigned to grazing and slaughtered unspecified is valid as a burnt offering, since the verse says “it is”: it shall remain in its being, meaning in what it is destined to be, a burnt offering, and from now on it is in that state; therefore even unspecified it is valid as a burnt offering and needs no uprooting. The halakha from Sinai was still needed, since without it we would not know what state it has. And according to the version in Pesaḥim (73a), “and he slaughtered it for the sake of a burnt offering, it is valid,” which implies that unspecified it is not valid because uprooting is needed, the reason is “it is”: it shall remain in its present state until he uproots it to a burnt offering; and the halakha from Sinai was still needed, since without it we would not have said that it is valid as a burnt offering even by uprooting. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a9.1: Even from their grazing [mimiraihu]: Rashi explained: even if they are at pasture in the meadow and the time of the Festival has come, he should not say, I will not trouble myself to seek them in the marsh and bring them, but I will wait until another time. Another version: even from their threshing-boards, meaning, even if they are threshing grain with threshing-boards. [End of his words.] This is not clear, since it was forbidden to work [a consecrated animal]. And the Ri explains “from their weakness” [mide’argaihu]: even if they are lean of flesh. For one might have thought that since they are weak he need not bring them up, since they are not the original consecration, such as offspring and substitutes; as for “for the oxen stumbled” (II Samuel 6:6), the Targum renders “for the oxen were weakened [itmerigu].” And Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Shneur explained “from their grazing”: even from a place where it is permitted to graze and raise it, that is, outside the Land, since one does not raise livestock in the Land of Israel. And this is the exposition in the Sifrei: “Only your holy things that you have”: from here, that one brings sacrificial animals from outside the Land. One might think the same is true of a firstborn and tithe; the verse states “only.” What did you see to include these and exclude those? After the verse included and excluded, I include these, which have no sustenance in their place, that is, they are not eaten in their blemished state outside the Land, and I exclude those, which have sustenance in their place, that is, they are eaten in their blemished state outside the Land.
tosafot:a10.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: The offspring of a peace offering is not sacrificed: and this is by rabbinic law, as the Gemara explains: lest he raise herds upon herds from it.
tosafot:a10.2: And the Rabbis say: It is sacrificed: this requires further study: the Rabbis are [the same as] the first tanna [of the previous mishna].
tosafot:a14.1: And its replacement: that is, it was lost, and he separated another in its place, and the first was found, and now both of them stand [before him].
tosafot:a16.1: Rabbi Shimon said: They do not disagree about the offspring [of the offspring] of a peace offering and about the offspring [of the offspring] of a substitute, that it is not sacrificed: the Amoraim in the Gemara disagree about this. Rabba said: It stands to reason that they do not disagree [such that one says] they are not sacrificed; rather, they are sacrificed. And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: They do not disagree [such that one says] they are sacrificed; rather, they are not sacrificed. And according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi there are three opinions in the matter. The first tanna, [before] Rabbi Shimon, holds that according to the first tanna [the Rabbis] all of them are sacrificed and according to Rabbi Eliezer none of them is sacrificed; and Rabbi Shimon holds that all agree that after the first offspring they are not sacrificed, and they disagree only about the first offspring. And the Gemara explains their reasons.
gershom:a1.1: If [it refers to] the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering: you cannot say the offspring of the guilt offering itself, since the guilt offering itself is a male and does not give birth.
gershom:a2.1: Actually, it refers to the offspring of a sin offering. And as for what you said, [but] it is learned that it dies: the halakha was learned for its death, and the verse “only” is to exclude it from being sacrificed. Rather, the halakha is for the offspring of a sin offering, and the verse “only” is needed [to teach] that if he transgressed and sacrificed the substitute of a guilt offering or its offspring, he stands in violation of a positive mitzva. And what positive mitzva is this? This “only” implies: these, yes, but not other sacrificial animals; that is a prohibition that comes by implication from a positive mitzva, [and a prohibition that comes by implication from a positive mitzva has the status of a positive mitzva.]
gershom:a3.1: [As Rav Huna said that Rav said:] A guilt offering that was consigned to grazing: for example, one separated a guilt offering to atone with it, and it was lost, and he separated another guilt offering and its owner achieved atonement, and afterward this one was found, and the treasurer said that it goes out to graze, and afterward one slaughtered it unspecified: it is valid [for the sake of] a burnt offering. [What is the reason it is valid for the sake of a burnt offering?] Because a guilt offering is a male and an offering of the most sacred order, and a burnt offering too is a male and of the most sacred order. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads “Rav Huna said that Rav said”; the daf has Rav Huna alone.]
gershom:a4.1: Consigned, yes; not consigned, no: that is, if, after it was consigned from the law of a guilt offering to grazing, he slaughtered it unspecified, it is valid for the sake of a burnt offering, since the name of a guilt offering is no longer on it. But if it was not consigned and he slaughtered it for the sake of a burnt offering, it is disqualified, [since it is] a disqualified guilt offering.
gershom:a5.1: What is the reason? Because the verse states “It is”: it shall remain in its present state. That is, since it was not consigned, even though he changed its name and slaughtered it for the sake of a burnt offering, it remains in its present state, and it is a disqualified guilt offering and is not sacrificed. But other offerings, about which “it is” is not written, whether consigned or not consigned, when one slaughtered them for the sake of another offering they are valid, except that they do not count for the owner [toward his obligation], as we learned: All offerings that were slaughtered not for their own sake, etc. [Zevaḥim 2a].
gershom:a6.1: And let him derive all of them: whether for the offspring of unblemished animals or of blemished animals, whether for the substitute of unblemished animals or of blemished animals.
gershom:a7.1: From “male” and from “female”: “if” he does not consider to imply anything to expound from it. Therefore he takes “male” and “female” for the offspring of blemished animals and for the substitute of blemished animals, and “only your holy things” for the offspring of unblemished animals and the substitute of unblemished animals, [deriving it] from “you shall take and go” and “you shall offer your burnt offerings,” since from there we derive that they are sacrificed.
gershom:a8.1: He would say to you: “You shall take and go” comes for this: once the Festival has arrived, you are not permitted to hold back from bringing your sacrificial animals and your vows immediately; rather, take them even from their threshing-boards [morigim]. That is, even if they went of their own accord onto the threshing floor, onto the grain and onto the threshing-boards, and are threshing, take them from there and bring them to the Temple. But intentionally it is forbidden to thresh with them, since that is labor. [Rabbeinu Gershom gives the “threshing” reading as the main answer and “grazing” as the other version, the reverse of the printed Gemara.]
gershom:a9.1: Another version: even from their grazing: if they are pasturing in the marsh in a distant place, he is obligated to go there and bring them.
gershom:a10.1: [“If”: a mother and not offspring. “If” implies a mother [em] and not an offspring. And its replacement: that is, he separated a substitute and it was lost, and he separated another in its place.
gershom:a11.1: A decree: that if you say the offspring of a peace offering is sacrificed,]
gershom:a12.1: Lest he raise herds upon herds from them: he will keep them back until he raises many from them, and perhaps he will come to a mishap, eating of them in the belief that they are non-sacred.
gershom:a13.1: They do not disagree about the offspring of a peace offering, nor about the offspring of a substitute: the offspring of a substitute is like the offspring of the offspring of a peace offering. And about what do they disagree? About the offspring itself [of a peace offering].
gershom:a14.1: How is it taught? [That] the Sages do not disagree about the offspring of the offspring, [saying] that it is sacrificed; rather, it is not sacrificed. And he took the end of the statement, that is, “it is sacrificed,” since about this they do not disagree. [The wording here is unclear. Rabbeinu Gershom’s first option is the “not sacrificed” reading, which the printed Gemara gives second.]
gershom:a15.1: Or perhaps this is how it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer does not disagree about the offspring of the offspring, [saying] that it is not sacrificed; rather, it is sacrificed. That is, we divide at the beginning of the statement, “it is not sacrificed,” [rather it is sacrificed]. For when Rabbi Eliezer decreed that it is not sacrificed, lest he raise herds from them, that was about the first offspring; but the offspring of the offspring is sacrificed, since they are already found to have generations, and since it is a second generation, people do not remember that it is the offspring of the offspring of a peace offering, and there is no concern lest he raise herds from them. [And some read: but about the offspring of the offspring he did not decree, since it is found only by mere chance; about the offspring of the offspring there is no concern.
gershom:a16.1: Because he has revealed his mind: since from his actions, that he left it until he had] an offspring of an offspring, his intention is evident that he wants it to raise herds; therefore it is not sacrificed.
rashi:b1.1: A lamb: implies the offspring of a lamb.
rashi:b2.1: “He” is sacrificed: the offspring of a peace offering, since the verse is written about peace offerings.
rashi:b3.1: The offspring of which: is he excluding, when you said “and the offspring of all sacrificial animals is not sacrificed”?
rashi:b4.1: The offspring of a tithe animal: an animal tithe that came out as the tenth and was a female, and afterward gave birth. Its offspring is not sacrificed; rather, it grazes and is eaten by its owners once blemished, like the law of the tithe, which is eaten by its owners once blemished.
rashi:b4.2: It is derived from the firstborn: and with a firstborn its offspring is not sacrificed, since a firstborn has no offspring, as it is a male.
rashi:b7.1: Each day he transgresses a positive mitzva: “And there you shall come… and there you shall bring” (Deuteronomy 12:5–6), which implies: on the first Festival on which you come there, bring all the vows that are upon you. [Rashi’s text reads “transgresses a positive mitzva,” where the printed Gemara has “You shall not delay.”]
rashi:b7.2: He must eat it from Shavuot: granted, on Passover they did not sacrifice it, since perhaps it was lacking in time: it was born on Passover, and the Festival passed before it was seven days old.
rashi:b8.1: And the other: Rav Zevid would say to you: wherever he teaches Passover and wishes to mention something about Shavuot, he teaches “Atzeret” and does not call it “ḥag.” But had he mentioned Passover with the term “the festival [ḥag] of matzot,” he would have taught Shavuot with the term “ḥag.”
rashi:b9.1: If so: that this ḥag is Shavuot, or that it was ill.
rashi:b9.2: What is his testimony: what does Rabbi Pappeyas come to teach us? Granted, if you say that this ḥag is Sukkot and on Shavuot it was not ill, Rabbi Pappeyas comes to exclude the view of Rava. But now, what do we learn from it?
rashi:b10.1: MISHNA: These are like a thanks offering: they are sacrificed and eaten for a day and a night.
rashi:b11.1: GEMARA: What does “he shall offer it” say: “If he offers it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer” etc. — since [the verse] could have written: “[If for a thanksgiving,] then he shall offer with the sacrifice of thanksgiving.”
rashi:b12.1: The verse states “he shall offer a thanks offering”: in any case.
rashi:b13.1: The second: if he sacrifices it after he has sacrificed the first.
rashi:b13.2: “Offer it”: one and not two: it is the loaves that it excludes, since it does not exclude the second from being sacrificed, as we derive [that it is sacrificed] from “if for a thanksgiving.”
rashi:b13.3: From where to include etc.: for sacrifice.
rashi:b13.4: And replacements: for example, it was lost and he separated another in its place.
rashi:b14.1: MISHNA: The substitute of a burnt offering: for example, he exchanged a male for a burnt offering.
rashi:b14.2: The offspring of a substitute: for example, if he exchanged a female for a burnt offering, and the substitute gave birth to a male.
rashi:b15.1: GEMARA: What is different: with the offspring of the substitute of a burnt offering, that the Rabbis do not disagree, since it states as the view of all: “these are” etc., and they are completely for the fire.
rashi:b15.2: And in the latter clause: about the offspring of a burnt offering the Rabbis disagree, [saying] that it itself is not sacrificed, only its money.
rashi:b16.1: It is taught as a dispute: just as they disagree at the end, so they disagree in the first clause, and the first clause, which teaches “these are like a burnt offering,” is Rabbi Elazar[’s view].
rashi:b16.2: With regard to the offspring of a substitute, its mother is sacrificed: not its actual mother; rather, the first consecration, by whose power all these came, is sacrificed, since it was a male. But with one who designates a female for a burnt offering, she was the first consecration, and she is not sacrificed.
rashi:b17.1: The substitute of a guilt offering: they graze, since it is a halakha to Moses from Sinai: in any case where a sin offering dies, with a guilt offering it grazes; and the substitute of a sin offering dies.
rashi:b17.2: For gift offerings: for the horns [the collection chests], from whose money communal gift offerings are sacrificed.
rashi:b18.1: They die: since he holds [that a guilt offering is] like a sin offering, at the beginning of tractate Zevaḥim (10b).
rashi:b18.2: He brings a burnt offering with their money: since surplus goes to an individual’s gift offering.
rashi:b18.3: It itself: the offspring of the substitute, no. Evidently, since its mother is not fit to be sacrificed as a burnt offering, as a female is not sacrificed as a burnt offering, and furthermore, even were it a male, it is learned that the substitute of a guilt offering grazes, therefore the offspring too is not sacrificed. Then with the offspring of a female burnt offering, why does he say that it is sacrificed?
rashi:b20.1: Since there is burnt offering status on its mother: one who designates an animal for a burnt offering, burnt offering status is upon it, since he consecrated it for a burnt offering. And if [you object] because it is a female, even so burnt offering status is upon it, since we find a female in the bird burnt offering. And furthermore, when it is sold, its money is a burnt offering, that is, for the sake of a burnt offering.
tosafot:b1.1: Rabbi Ḥiyya teaches to support Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: “If he offers a lamb”: the first offspring is sacrificed, the second offspring is not sacrificed: and this is necessarily according to the Rabbis, since according to Rabbi Eliezer the first offspring is not sacrificed at all. And this exposition is merely a supporting allusion [asmakhta], since certainly the rule that the second offspring is not sacrificed is rabbinic, lest he raise herds upon herds from it. And in Pesaḥim (96b) this verse is applied to a different exposition.
tosafot:b7.1: He must eat it from Shavuot: but he does not object that he must eat it from Passover, since it is possible that it was lacking in time.
tosafot:b9.1: If so, what is his testimony: granted, if it was not ill on Shavuot and this refers to the festival of Sukkot, Rabbi Pappeyas comes to exclude the view of Rava; but now, what does he teach us?
tosafot:b13.1: And replacements: this requires further study: what are replacements? For if he separated a thanks offering and it was lost, and he separated another in its place, and the first was found, and both of them stand, we already heard this from the beginning of the baraita.
tosafot:b16.1: But with regard to the offspring of a substitute, whose mother is also sacrificed: not its actual mother; rather, the first consecration, by whose power these came, and it is sacrificed, since it is a male.
tosafot:b18.1: With their money, yes; it itself, no: And if you will say: what does this teach us? Perhaps it is different here, that it is not sacrificed, because in any case where a sin offering dies, with a guilt offering it grazes; the offspring of a sin offering dies, and therefore with a guilt offering it grazes, but it itself is not sacrificed. One can say: “with a guilt offering it grazes” was established only for those cases that apply to a guilt offering in its proper way, such as its owner died, or achieved atonement, or a substitute, or its year passed; all these four apply to a guilt offering in its proper way. But the offspring of a guilt offering is not in its proper way, since a guilt offering is a male and offspring does not apply to it; for this the halakha was not established.
tosafot:b19.1: But according to you, who say it is not sacrificed: And if you will say: then there is a contradiction between the Rabbis and the Rabbis, according to what Rava said above, that where its mother is sacrificed even the Rabbis concede that the offspring too is sacrificed. Here, with the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering, its mother is sacrificed; if so, they should have said that the offspring itself is sacrificed. One can say: Rav Ḥisda here does not accept Rava’s answer above, but holds like the answer of Rabba bar bar Ḥana, that it is taught as a dispute and the first clause is Rabbi Elazar’s. And Rava, who answered above that where its mother is sacrificed even the Rabbis concede, answers here differently, as follows shortly, where Rava gives another answer. And my teacher, the RaMaR, explained that Rav Ḥisda can indeed accept Rava’s answer above: when he says that where its mother is sacrificed even the Rabbis concede, that applies to the offspring of the substitute of a burnt offering, where the principal original consecration is sacrificed as a burnt offering, so it is right that the offspring itself be sacrificed as a burnt offering. But here, with the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering, the principal original consecration is sacrificed as a guilt offering and not as a burnt offering, so it is not right that the offspring be sacrificed as a burnt offering. And though he says according to Rabbi Elazar, about one who designates a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth, that even though the principal is not sacrificed as a burnt offering but grazes, the offspring itself is sacrificed, so too he should have said about the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering: even though the principal consecration is not sacrificed as a burnt offering, the offspring itself is sacrificed. [So explained] my teacher, the RaMaR.
tosafot:b20.1: Rather, with one who designates a female for a burnt offering, since there is burnt offering status on its mother: Rashi’s wording: since he consecrated it for a burnt offering; and if because it is a female, even so burnt offering status is upon it, since we find a female in the bird burnt offering; and furthermore, when they are sold, its money is a burnt offering, that is, burnt offering status. But the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering has no burnt offering status on it, since its mother has none, neither it nor its money. [End of his words.] And the first explanation, that burnt offering status is on its mother because of the bird burnt offering, cannot stand in the discussion below, and I will explain it in its place.
gershom:b1.1: “If he offers a lamb”: [the verse] did not need to write “And if he brings a lamb as his offering, he shall present it before the Lord”; rather, “he offers” comes for this: that it, the first offspring, is sacrificed; the offspring of the offspring is not sacrificed.
gershom:b2.1: The offspring of which: of other sacrificial animals did [the verse] need to exclude? If of a burnt offering and a guilt offering, etc.
gershom:b3.1: [Ravina said: To include the offspring of a tithe animal, that it is not sacrificed. Just as with a firstborn its offspring is not sacrificed, since it is not capable of offspring, as a firstborn is a male.
gershom:b4.1: It is necessary: “he” [is needed] to exclude the offspring of tithe. For it might enter your mind to say: one does not derive the possible, the tithe, which applies to females too, and they have offspring, from the firstborn, where it is impossible, since it has no offspring; and so the offspring of tithe would be sacrificed. It teaches us: “he,” and not the offspring of other sacrificial animals.
gershom:b5.1: For example, the offspring was ill on Shavuot, so that it was not fit to be sacrificed.]
gershom:b6.1: What is the ḥag that is taught? “And we ate its offspring as a peace offering on the Festival [beḥag]”: on Shavuot, which is a festival.
gershom:b7.1: And Rav Zevid said: if this were speaking of Shavuot, he would have called it “the festival of weeks”; but since he said “on the Festival” unspecified, that is Sukkot. And the reason they did not sacrifice it on Shavuot is that it was ill.
gershom:b8.1: If so: since that is why they did not sacrifice it, because it was ill, had it been healthy they would have sacrificed it on Shavuot. If so, what is the purpose of Rabbi Pappeyas’s testimony? What novelty did he teach us in saying “and we ate it on the Festival”? Perhaps the reason is that it was ill on Shavuot. Rather, this is the novelty he teaches us: to exclude the view of Rabbi Eliezer.
gershom:b9.1: [What does “he shall offer a thanks offering” say? That is, this “he shall offer it” in “if for a thanksgiving” is entirely superfluous, since it could have said: “And if for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the sacrifice of thanksgiving.”
gershom:b10.1: Rather, what does the verse teach by “he shall offer”? You learn about one who separates his thanks offering, etc.
gershom:b11.1: Replacements: that is, it was lost and he separated another in its place.
gershom:b12.1: The verse states “And if for a thanksgiving”: it included that substitute, offspring and replacements are also a thanks offering.]
gershom:b13.1: The substitute of a burnt offering: for example, a female substitute was exchanged for a male burnt offering [and that female substitute gave birth].
gershom:b14.1: Their offspring [a marginal gloss suggests reading: and the offspring of the substitute that gave birth, the offspring of their offspring, etc.]: that is, the offspring of a substitute, the offspring [that] the substitute [bore], the offspring of their offspring until the end of the world, these are like a burnt offering. And even though that substitute is a female, which is not fit for a burnt offering, it is sanctified, [as was said] in the first chapter: one may substitute males for females and females for males.
gershom:b15.1: [One who designates a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth to a male: it grazes until it becomes unfit and is sold,] and he brings a burnt offering with its money: for communal gift offerings. And for this reason it grazes: because it comes from the power of a sanctity that is not fit, since a female is not fit for a burnt offering, and all the more so its mother grazes.
gershom:b16.1: Rabbi Elazar says: It itself: the offspring shall not graze but shall be sacrificed as a burnt offering.
gershom:b17.1: [What is different in the first clause: that the Rabbis do not disagree about the substitute of a burnt offering and the offspring of the substitute, but agree that these are like a burnt offering, which are sacrificed.
gershom:b18.1: And what is different in the latter clause: about one who designates a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth to a male, that they disagree, saying it grazes.
gershom:b19.1: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:] It is taught as a dispute: [just as they disagree] in the latter clause, they disagree in the first clause; and what is taught, “these are like a burnt offering,” is Rabbi Eliezer[’s view] and not the Rabbis’. [So Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads Rabbi Elazar.]
gershom:b20.1: Since its mother is not sacrificed: as a burnt offering, since it is a female; therefore they say its offspring grazes.
gershom:b21.1: But with regard to the offspring of the substitute of a burnt offering: whose mother is sacrificed, [the mother of the offspring of the substitute]; he calls the burnt offering itself the “mother” of the substitute, since the substitute comes from its power. Even the Rabbis concede that their offspring are like a burnt offering.
gershom:b22.1: Another version: “and completely to the fire” [is the view of all, and raise a contradiction, etc. Rav Huna said: It is taught as a dispute; as in the first clause, so in the latter clause; and “completely to the fire” is not the view of all but is Rabbi Elazar’s. [This version names Rav Huna where the daf has Rabba bar bar Ḥana.]
gershom:b23.1: You may even say: and with the substitute of a burnt offering they do not disagree with Rabbi Elazar, since the female substitute of a burnt offering] is secondary to that first one, for the substitute is the secondary one, and the first one, which he separated [before he separated the substitute], was a principal burnt offering; he separated a male. [Therefore] the Rabbis did not penalize the offspring of the substitute, but said that it is sacrificed.
gershom:b24.1: But one who designates a female for a burnt offering, etc. And their offspring: the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering, the offspring of its offspring. And their money goes to gift offerings: to the horns [the collection chests], that is, to communal gift offerings.
gershom:b25.1: Rabbi Elazar says: It grazes and is sold, and he brings a burnt offering with their money: for an individual’s gift offering. But he does not bring a guilt offering with their money, as we say below that the surplus of a guilt offering is not sacrificed as a guilt offering but grazes; the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering also grazes, and he brings a burnt offering with its money. [With its money he brings one, but it itself is not sacrificed.]
gershom:b26.1: Concede to me at least that the surplus: the offspring are the surplus.
gershom:b27.1: Goes to an individual’s gift offering: as we say at the end of the first chapter, that Rabbi Elazar holds that surplus goes to an individual’s gift offering and renders a substitute, and the Rabbis say to him: surplus goes to communal gift offerings, and a burnt offering that comes from surplus does not render a substitute, since there is no substitution for a community.
gershom:b28.1: Rava said: You may even say that Rabbi Elazar said of the offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering that certainly it itself is not sacrificed, and what he says of the offspring of a burnt offering, that it itself is sacrificed, is no difficulty, because there is burnt offering status on its mother, since we find a female burnt offering for a poor person, in the bird burnt offering. But with the substitute of a guilt offering we find nothing like burnt offering status on its mother, since we do not find [any] female in a guilt offering. Therefore Rabbi Elazar concedes: with its money, yes, but it itself is not sacrificed.
gershom:b29.1: Another version: [the offspring at least, since it is seen to be a male, is itself sacrificed.]
gershom:b30.1: You may even say Rabbi Elazar: when it is taught, one who designates a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth to a male, it itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering, since there is burnt offering status on its mother, as we said, sanctity descended on its body. And furthermore, it is not his obligatory burnt offering but a voluntary one [a gift]; and since he could discharge himself with a bird burnt offering, as Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who says below: one who says “It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering” brings a lamb; Rabbi Elazar says: he brings a turtledove or a young pigeon [the names here appear confused], sanctity descended on its body, [and therefore] the offspring too is sanctified in its body and is sacrificed. But with the substitute of a guilt offering, where there is no guilt offering status on its mother, as we said, and since a guilt offering is his obligation, and he cannot bring a female for his guilt offering, and if he brings a female for his guilt offering it is sanctified only for its value, the offspring too is not sanctified in its body; rather, it is sold and he brings a burnt offering with its money.
